questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Under the Electronic Commerce Act (RA 8792), which statement best describes what the law sets out to do?

choices.A: Require every government office to replace all its paper records with electronic files
choices.B: Give electronic dealings legal effect and trust, in government and private life alike
choices.C: Fix the prices that online sellers may charge Filipino consumers on the internet
choices.D: Punish every misuse of computers, from spam messages to identity theft and fraud

questions.explanation:
**B is correct.** The Act's declared aims (Sec. 3) are to make dealings, contracts and the storage of information possible through electronic and similar means, to recognize electronic documents as authentic and reliable, and to promote electronic transactions in government and among the public. Its point is enabling: it removes legal doubt about doing things electronically, so that people and offices can rely on electronic records the way they rely on paper. Everything else in the Act, from the rules on writing and signatures to the rules on e-government, serves that aim. So the best description is that the law gives electronic dealings legal effect and trust.

**A is wrong:** the Act asks government to be able to accept and issue electronic documents, but it never abolishes paper; enabling a choice is different from forcing a switch.

**C is wrong:** price regulation is not part of the Act at all; it deals with the legal recognition of electronic records and transactions, not with what sellers charge.

**D is wrong:** the Act penalizes a few specific acts, such as hacking and piracy, but it is not a general cybercrime code; treating it as one confuses it with later, broader laws.

**Watch for:** If a question asks which law makes an electronic contract valid, the answer is this Act; if it asks which law punishes a wide range of online crimes, look beyond it.

**Basis:** RA 8792, Sec. 3. Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra2000/ra_8792_2000.html.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Under the Electronic Commerce Act (RA 8792), a lawmaker proposes that the State itself fund and run most of the country's ICT businesses. How does this proposal fit the policy the law declares?

choices.A: Well, because the policy makes the State the main investor in and owner of ICT businesses
choices.B: Poorly, because the policy expects private firms to lead ICT investment, with the State supporting
choices.C: Well, because the policy keeps private firms out of building national ICT networks
choices.D: It does not matter, because the law says nothing at all about who should invest in ICT

questions.explanation:
**B is correct.** The Act's declaration of policy treats information and communications technology as essential to nation-building, and it assigns roles: private enterprise is expected to be the main source of investment, while the State supports it. The State's part is to build an ICT-skilled workforce, encourage technology transfer, keep networks secure and neutral, and develop national information infrastructure linked to global networks. A plan for the State to fund and run most ICT businesses reverses those roles. It therefore sits poorly with the declared policy.

**A is wrong:** this flips the policy; the State is cast as an enabler and regulator, not as the main investor or owner.

**C is wrong:** nothing in the policy excludes private firms; on the contrary, it relies on them to drive investment.

**D is wrong:** the declaration of policy expressly speaks to investment and to the State's supporting role, so the law is not silent.

**Basis:** RA 8792, Sec. 2. Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra2000/ra_8792_2000.html.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Under the Electronic Commerce Act (RA 8792), Rosa lent money to her cousin and wants to use their personal text messages about the loan in court. The cousin argues that the law covers only business dealings. Is he right?

choices.A: Yes, because messages between relatives fall outside the law when no business is involved
choices.B: Yes, because the law applies only when at least one party is a registered business entity
choices.C: No, because the law reaches data messages in personal as well as commercial dealings
choices.D: No, but only because the loan is large enough to count as a commercial transaction

questions.explanation:
**C is correct.** The Act's scope (Sec. 4) covers any kind of data message or electronic document used in commercial or non-commercial activities, whether domestic or international. Personal communications are expressly among the non-commercial uses, alongside government forms and information storage. The word “commerce” in the title describes the law's main motivation, not a limit on its reach. Rosa's text messages are data messages about a private loan, so they fall within the Act and the cousin's argument fails.

**A is wrong:** this reads the law's title as its scope; the scope clause includes non-commercial activities such as personal communications.

**B is wrong:** no such registration requirement exists in the scope clause; it looks at the kind of record, not at who the parties are.

**D is wrong:** the amount is irrelevant; even a small personal loan is covered because personal communications are within the scope.

**Watch for:** The same messages would also be covered if the cousin lived abroad, because the scope includes international as well as domestic dealings.

**Basis:** RA 8792, Sec. 4. Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra2000/ra_8792_2000.html.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Under the Electronic Commerce Act (RA 8792), a company signs a supply contract through an e-signing platform instead of on paper. If the law's requirements are met, how is the electronic contract treated?

choices.A: As a weaker contract a court may enforce only if no paper copy exists
choices.B: As having the same legal effect as a paper contract signed by hand
choices.C: As a draft that binds only after both sides print it and sign it by hand
choices.D: As valid between the parties but never usable as evidence in a court case

questions.explanation:
**B is correct.** Functional equivalence means that once the Act's requirements are satisfied, an electronic document or signature does the same legal job as its paper counterpart. The principle exists so that the medium, by itself, never decides whether a transaction counts. It is conditional: the electronic record must meet the requirements, for example on integrity and on signatures. Here the requirements are assumed to be met, so the e-signed contract has the same effect as one signed by hand on paper.

**A is wrong:** the principle gives equal, not second-class, effect; there is no rule that paper must be looked for first.

**C is wrong:** requiring a printed, hand-signed copy would defeat the whole point of functional equivalence.

**D is wrong:** the Act recognizes electronic documents for evidentiary purposes too; equivalence is precisely what lets them be used in court.

**Watch for:** If the facts said the requirements were not met (for example, the file was later altered), equivalence would not attach, and the answer would change.

**Basis:** RA 8792, Sec. 7. Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra2000/ra_8792_2000.html.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Under the Electronic Commerce Act (RA 8792), a buyer refuses to honor an order sent through a messaging app, arguing that only orders sent through one specific business email service are legally recognized. Which principle defeats this argument?

choices.A: Functional equivalence, since electronic orders must first be printed to have effect
choices.B: Non-discrimination, since only courts may decide which platforms are acceptable
choices.C: Confidentiality, since messages sent through apps are private and protected
choices.D: Technological neutrality, since the law does not prefer any particular platform

questions.explanation:
**D is correct.** Technological neutrality means the law does not favor any brand, product or technology. What matters is whether the record qualifies as a data message or electronic document, not which app, operating system or service produced it. The principle keeps the law from becoming outdated or from picking commercial winners. A messaging-app order qualifies as a data message, so the buyer cannot insist on one email service.

**A is wrong:** functional equivalence concerns electronic records standing in for paper; it does not require printing, and it does not address which platform is used.

**B is wrong:** non-discrimination bars denying effect to a record just because it is electronic; it does not hand courts the power to approve platforms.

**C is wrong:** confidentiality governs who may access and share electronic records, not whether an order sent through an app is legally recognized.

**Watch for:** If the parties had expressly agreed beforehand to use only one channel for orders, their agreement, not neutrality, would decide the issue.

**Basis:** RA 8792, Sec. 2 (neutrality of technology). Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra2000/ra_8792_2000.html.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Under the Electronic Commerce Act (RA 8792), a judge refuses to consider a lease agreement solely because the parties never had it on paper and kept it only as a computer file. Which principle does the judge violate?

choices.A: Technological neutrality, since the judge must accept files from every software brand
choices.B: Non-discrimination, since a record cannot be denied effect only for being electronic
choices.C: The best evidence rule, since the judge must always demand the paper original first
choices.D: Party autonomy, since the parties alone decide what evidence the court may consider

questions.explanation:
**B is correct.** Non-discrimination (Sec. 6) bars denying information legal effect, validity or enforceability on the sole ground that it is in electronic form. It exists so that courts and agencies give electronic records the same weight as paper ones, instead of treating the medium as a defect. The judge's only reason for refusing the lease is that it exists only as a file. That is exactly the ground the principle forbids.

**A is wrong:** neutrality is about not favoring a brand or technology; the judge here rejected the record because it was electronic at all, not because of its brand.

**C is wrong:** the Act adjusts the best evidence rule for electronic documents; it does not make paper the required first choice.

**D is wrong:** parties do not control what a court may receive; and party autonomy is not the principle that addresses this refusal.

**Watch for:** If the judge had refused the file because its integrity was doubtful, that would be a question of reliability, not discrimination, and could be proper.

**Basis:** RA 8792, Sec. 6. Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra2000/ra_8792_2000.html.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Under the Electronic Commerce Act (RA 8792), why is it a mistake to assume that an electronic document admitted in evidence also proves a valid transaction?

choices.A: Admission only lets the court receive it; validity depends on the deal's own requisites and form
choices.B: Admitted documents are always valid, so there is no mistake in the assumption
choices.C: Validity is first decided by the DTI, and courts may only rule on admissibility
choices.D: Electronic documents can be valid but are never admissible, so the issue cannot arise

questions.explanation:
**A is correct.** Validity and admissibility are separate questions. Admissibility asks whether the court may receive the electronic document as evidence; validity asks whether the transaction itself meets its essential requisites and any form the law requires. The Act mainly helps with proof: an electronic record can be received and weighed like paper. But receiving a record in evidence cannot cure a missing requirement of the transaction, so admission never settles validity by itself.

**B is wrong:** this merges the two questions; a perfectly admissible email can still show a transaction that lacks a required form.

**C is wrong:** the DTI does not decide the validity of private transactions; courts decide both questions.

**D is wrong:** electronic documents are admissible under the Act and the Rules on Electronic Evidence; the problem is the opposite assumption.

**Watch for:** In any problem, first ask which issue is being tested: if the question is whether a contract exists, think validity; if it is whether a court can look at the email, think admissibility.

**Basis:** RA 8792, Secs. 7 (proviso) and 12. Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra2000/ra_8792_2000.html.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Under the Electronic Commerce Act (RA 8792), a courier company that receives and forwards electronic documents for its clients acts, as to those documents, as an ____.
questions.fullText: Under the Electronic Commerce Act (RA 8792), a courier company that receives and forwards electronic documents for its clients acts, as to those documents, as an intermediary.
questions.explanation:
**Answer:** intermediary.

**Why:** The Act distinguishes the people involved in an electronic document by their role. The originator is the person who creates or sends the document on its own account; the addressee is the person it is meant for; and an intermediary handles the document for someone else, by sending, receiving or storing it on that person's behalf. The courier company forwards its clients' documents, so it acts for others. That makes it an intermediary.

**Not to be confused with:** “originator.” A student may pick it because the courier physically sends the documents, but the Act excludes intermediaries from the definition of originator: sending on behalf of another does not make the courier the author.

**Watch for:** If the courier sent its own invoice to a client, it would be the originator of that document.

**Basis:** RA 8792, Sec. 5(h)–(i). Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra2000/ra_8792_2000.html.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Under the Electronic Commerce Act (RA 8792), Atty. Reyes drafts a demand letter and has his secretary email it from the firm's account to Mr. Cruz. Who is the originator of the electronic document?

choices.A: The secretary, because she was the one who pressed send
choices.B: Mr. Cruz, because the letter was written for him to read
choices.C: Atty. Reyes, who wrote the letter and had it sent for him
choices.D: The email provider, because it carried the message across

questions.explanation:
**C is correct.** The originator is the person who creates or sends the electronic document, but the Act expressly excludes an intermediary from that role. An intermediary is someone who sends, receives or stores an electronic document on behalf of another. The secretary pressed send, but she did so for Atty. Reyes, which makes her an intermediary. The letter is Atty. Reyes's document, so he is the originator.

**A is wrong:** pressing send for someone else is the classic intermediary role, which the definition of originator excludes.

**B is wrong:** Mr. Cruz is the addressee, the person the document is intended for, not its originator.

**D is wrong:** the provider is a service provider that transmits the message; it neither authors nor sends it on its own account.

**Watch for:** If the secretary had written and sent her own letter from her account, she would be the originator of that letter.

**Basis:** RA 8792, Sec. 5(a), (h) and (i). Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra2000/ra_8792_2000.html.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Under the Electronic Commerce Act (RA 8792), a cloud company that only stores clients' contracts on its servers, with no right to change their contents unless authorized, is acting as a ____.
questions.fullText: Under the Electronic Commerce Act (RA 8792), a cloud company that only stores clients' contracts on its servers, with no right to change their contents unless authorized, is acting as a service provider.
questions.explanation:
**Answer:** service provider.

**Why:** A service provider is an entity that offers online services, network access or the technical means to store or transmit electronic documents. Because it is only the channel or the storage, it has no authority to change the content of what it carries unless it is authorized to do so. The cloud company stores contracts for clients and may not edit them, which fits that role exactly. So the correct term is service provider.

**Not to be confused with:** “intermediary.” Both handle documents for others, but an intermediary sends, receives or stores a particular document on someone's behalf, while a service provider offers the general service or infrastructure (network access, storage, transmission) that many users rely on.

**Watch for:** Whether a service provider can be held liable for what passes through it is a separate question with its own conditions (Sec. 30); verify the current rule.

**Basis:** RA 8792, Secs. 5(j) and 30. Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra2000/ra_8792_2000.html.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Under the Electronic Commerce Act (RA 8792), Mia gets two things from a furniture store: a chat notice that her order went through, and an emailed PDF of the signed sales agreement. How should each be classified?

choices.A: The chat notice is a data message; the emailed agreement is an electronic document
choices.B: Both are electronic documents, since anything sent by phone or email is a document
choices.C: The chat notice is an electronic document; the emailed agreement is a data message
choices.D: Neither is covered, since only notarized electronic files are recognized by law

questions.explanation:
**A is correct.** A data message is any information generated, sent, received or stored by electronic or similar means (Sec. 5(c)). An electronic document is narrower: it is information that creates a right, ends an obligation or serves to prove a fact (Sec. 5(f)). A notice that an order went through is simply information sent electronically, the typical data message. The signed sales agreement establishes rights and obligations, so it is an electronic document; and both can still evidence an electronic contract.

**B is wrong:** this ignores the narrower definition of electronic document; not every message establishes rights or proves facts in the legal sense.

**C is wrong:** this reverses the categories; the signed agreement is the one that creates rights and obligations.

**D is wrong:** notarization is not a condition for coverage; the Act covers ordinary data messages and electronic documents.

**Watch for:** In evidence the distinction matters little, because the Rules on Electronic Evidence treat the two interchangeably.

**Basis:** RA 8792, Sec. 5(c) and (f). Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra2000/ra_8792_2000.html.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Under the Electronic Commerce Act (RA 8792), Ben keeps a digital receipt of a purchase on his phone and never prints it. Is it an electronic document?

choices.A: No, because a record becomes a document only once it is printed on paper
choices.B: No, because a receipt does not create any right or prove any fact by itself
choices.C: Yes, because what counts is the information it holds, not whether it is on paper
choices.D: Yes, but only if the store attached a digital signature to the receipt file

questions.explanation:
**C is correct.** An electronic document is information, kept or handled electronically, that creates a right, ends an obligation or serves to prove a fact (Sec. 5(f)). The definition looks at the content and its legal use, not at paper or format. A receipt records that a sale took place and what was paid, so it can prove a fact. Kept on Ben's phone, it is therefore an electronic document even though it was never printed.

**A is wrong:** printing is irrelevant; the definition is built around electronic production and storage, not paper.

**B is wrong:** a receipt is evidence of payment and of the purchase, which is precisely proving a fact.

**D is wrong:** a digital signature affects how strongly the document can be authenticated, not whether it is an electronic document at all.

**Watch for:** A printout of the receipt is a separate question: in evidence, a printout that accurately reflects the data is treated as an original.

**Basis:** RA 8792, Sec. 5(f). Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra2000/ra_8792_2000.html.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Under the Electronic Commerce Act (RA 8792) and the Rules on Electronic Evidence, a party offers a text message in court, and the other side objects that it is only a “data message,” not an “electronic document.” Should the objection succeed?

choices.A: Yes; only electronic documents, never data messages, may be offered in evidence
choices.B: No; in evidence the two kinds of electronic record are treated as interchangeable
choices.C: Yes; a text message must first be printed and notarized before it is offered
choices.D: No; a text message becomes a paper document once it is displayed on a phone

questions.explanation:
**B is correct.** The Act defines a data message broadly, as any information sent or stored electronically, and an electronic document more narrowly, as information that establishes a right, extinguishes an obligation or proves a fact (Sec. 5). Outside the courtroom the distinction can matter, but the Rules on Electronic Evidence (Rule 2) treat the two terms interchangeably for purposes of evidence. The objection rests entirely on the label. Since the label makes no difference in evidence, the objection should be overruled.

**A is wrong:** the Rules on Electronic Evidence make the two interchangeable, so a data message is not excluded for being a data message.

**C is wrong:** neither printing nor notarization is a condition for offering a text message; authentication is what is needed.

**D is wrong:** the right result, but for the wrong reason: a message shown on a screen is still electronic, not paper.

**Watch for:** If the objection were instead that the message was never authenticated, it would raise a real issue, because electronic evidence must still be authenticated.

**Basis:** RA 8792, Sec. 5; Rules on Electronic Evidence, Rule 2, Sec. 1(h). Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra2000/ra_8792_2000.html, https://lawphil.net/courts/supreme/am/am_01-7-01_2001.html.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Under the Electronic Commerce Act (RA 8792), Carlo types his full name at the end of an email agreeing to a deal. Dana signs a government e-filing with a signature that relies on encryption keys. Which statement is correct?

choices.A: Both used digital signatures, because both were made using a computer or a phone
choices.B: Carlo's typed name is not a signature at all, so only Dana's signing has effect
choices.C: Carlo used an electronic signature; Dana used a digital signature, a more secure type
choices.D: Dana's is not an electronic signature, because encryption takes it outside the law

questions.explanation:
**C is correct.** An electronic signature is any mark, sound or method in electronic form that identifies a person and is attached to a record with the intention of signing or approving it (Sec. 5(e)); a typed name can qualify. A digital signature is a particular kind of electronic signature that uses a pair of encryption keys, which lets others check both who signed and whether the record was changed. Every digital signature is an electronic signature, but not the other way around. So Carlo's typed name is an electronic signature, and Dana's key-based signature is a digital signature.

**A is wrong:** using a device does not make a signature digital; a digital signature specifically relies on encryption keys.

**B is wrong:** a typed name can be an electronic signature; whether it equals a handwritten one depends on the Sec. 8 requirements.

**D is wrong:** encryption does not remove a signature from the law; a digital signature is a subset of electronic signatures.

**Watch for:** Whether Carlo's typed name has the full effect of a handwritten signature is a different question, decided by the Sec. 8 requirements, not by the label.

**Basis:** RA 8792, Sec. 5(e); Rules on Electronic Evidence, Rule 2, Sec. 1(a) and (j). Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra2000/ra_8792_2000.html, https://lawphil.net/courts/supreme/am/am_01-7-01_2001.html.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Under the Electronic Commerce Act (RA 8792), an emailed contract is offered to satisfy a legal requirement that the agreement be in writing. Which of these events would most likely defeat that?

choices.A: One party quietly changed the price in the file after both sides had agreed to it
choices.B: The email system stamped the date and time on the message when it was delivered
choices.C: Both parties later added an agreed remark confirming that the contract was received
choices.D: The file was moved to a new folder when the company upgraded its email servers

questions.explanation:
**A is correct.** An electronic document satisfies a requirement of writing if it keeps its integrity and reliability and can be authenticated for later reference (Sec. 7(a)). Integrity means the document has stayed complete and unaltered, with some changes allowed: endorsements, authorized changes, and changes that happen naturally when a record is sent, stored or displayed. The test protects what the parties actually agreed on, while tolerating harmless technical changes. A secret change to the price alters the agreed terms, so the file no longer has the integrity the writing requirement needs.

**B is wrong:** a delivery time-stamp is a change that arises in the ordinary course of communication, which the rule expressly tolerates.

**C is wrong:** an endorsement or authorized change does not break integrity; only unauthorized alteration does.

**D is wrong:** moving a file during storage changes where it is kept, not what it says; that is a normal storage change.

**Watch for:** If the price change had been agreed by both parties and recorded, it would be an authorized change and the writing requirement could still be met.

**Basis:** RA 8792, Sec. 7(a). Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra2000/ra_8792_2000.html.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Under the Electronic Commerce Act (RA 8792), a regulation requires a company to present its invoices in their original form during an audit, but the company kept them only as electronic files. What must it show for the files to satisfy the requirement?

choices.A: Reliable assurance of their integrity since final form, and that they can be displayed
choices.B: That they were printed the day they were made and signed by a company officer
choices.C: That the auditor agreed beforehand to accept electronic files instead of paper
choices.D: Nothing more, since electronic files always count as originals in any audit

questions.explanation:
**A is correct.** Where a law requires a document to be presented or kept in its original form, an electronic document satisfies it on two conditions. First, there must be reliable assurance that the document's integrity has been kept from the time it was first generated in its final form. Second, the person who must see it has to be able to view it on a screen or in some other form. The company must therefore show both: that the invoice files have not been altered since they were finalized, and that the auditor can view them.

**B is wrong:** printing and signing are not conditions; the rule is built around integrity and the ability to display.

**C is wrong:** the rule does not depend on the other side's consent; it sets objective conditions the files must meet.

**D is wrong:** equivalence is conditional; a file whose integrity cannot be assured does not satisfy an original-form requirement.

**Watch for:** Verify the current section number: one set of materials places this rule in Sec. 7(c), another in Sec. 10.

**Also note:** Both Sec. 7(c) (for electronic documents) and Sec. 10 (for data messages and electronic documents) state this original-form rule.

**Basis:** RA 8792, Secs. 7(c) and 10. Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra2000/ra_8792_2000.html.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Under the Electronic Commerce Act (RA 8792), another law requires a particular formality for a certain kind of contract to be valid. If the parties make that contract electronically, what is the effect of RA 8792 on the formality?

choices.A: It removes the formality, since electronic contracts are exempt from such rules
choices.B: It replaces the formality with an e-signature, which is always enough by itself
choices.C: It suspends the formality until the DTI issues rules for that kind of contract
choices.D: None; the Act leaves formalities that other laws require for validity untouched

questions.explanation:
**D is correct.** The Act recognizes electronic documents and signatures, but it contains an express limit: none of its provisions changes what existing laws require as formalities for a document's validity. The limit preserves rules that exist for protection, such as public instruments and notarization. An electronic version of the contract can therefore help prove it, but it cannot excuse a formality the other law makes essential. The formality still has to be complied with.

**A is wrong:** the Act's proviso says the opposite: existing formality requirements are not varied.

**B is wrong:** an e-signature can stand for a signature, but it cannot supply a different formality such as a public instrument.

**C is wrong:** there is no such suspension and no DTI power to waive formalities required by other laws.

**Watch for:** Which documents still need a physically signed paper version (for example, checks, promissory notes or powers of attorney) is a separate question; verify the current rule.

**Basis:** RA 8792, Sec. 7 (proviso). Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra2000/ra_8792_2000.html.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Under the Electronic Commerce Act (RA 8792), Tomas, who works abroad, sends his sister an email saying she may sell his house and lot in Laguna on his behalf. She finds a buyer. The buyer's lawyer questions whether the sister has valid authority. Advise the buyer.

suggestedAnswer.answer: The buyer should not rely on the email alone. An agent's authority to sell land is subject to a special form requirement, and the e-commerce law does not relax such requirements.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Under the Civil Code, when a sale of land is made through an agent, the agent's authority must be in writing (Art. 1874); otherwise the sale is void. RA 8792 lets an electronic document satisfy a requirement of writing (Sec. 7), but it also states that it does not vary formalities that other laws require for validity. Authority to sell land is commonly listed among the documents that must still be physically written and signed; verify the current rule on whether an electronic document can satisfy it.
suggestedAnswer.application: The sister's only authority is an email from Tomas. Because the sale involves land, her authority is subject to the special form rule, and a defect in that authority would make the sale vulnerable. The safer course is for the buyer to require a written, signed (and, in practice, properly executed) authority from Tomas before paying or signing.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion:
Advise the buyer to require a properly executed written authority from Tomas; the email by itself is not a safe basis for the sale.

**Common mistake:** treating the case as a pure e-commerce question (an email is writing, so it is fine) and forgetting the special form rule for an agent's authority to sell land.

**Watch for:** If the property were a car instead of land, the special rule on an agent's authority to sell land would not apply, and the analysis would change.

**Also note:** Whether an email can satisfy the Art. 1874 writing requirement is not settled in the statute itself; check the current rule and any decisions before relying on it.

**Basis:** Civil Code, Art. 1874; RA 8792, Sec. 7. Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra2000/ra_8792_2000.html, https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra1949/ra_386_1949.html.

keyPoints: Sale of land through an agent: authority must be in writing (Art. 1874)
RA 8792 lets electronic documents satisfy writing, but does not vary other laws' formalities for validity
Authority to sell land is commonly treated as needing a physically written, signed document (verify)
Practical advice: require a properly executed written authority before proceeding

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Under the Electronic Commerce Act (RA 8792), a deed that the law requires to be in a public instrument is signed by both parties with electronic signatures and is never notarized. Do the electronic signatures make it a public instrument?

choices.A: Yes; an e-signature has the same effect as notarization under the e-commerce law
choices.B: Yes, but only if both parties used digital signatures backed by public-key certificates
choices.C: No; e-signatures are never valid, so the deed has no effect of any kind at all
choices.D: No; where a public instrument is required, an e-signature alone cannot supply it

questions.explanation:
**D is correct.** An electronic signature can stand in for a handwritten signature if the Sec. 8 requirements are met. But a public instrument is more than a signed document: it requires the formalities of notarization or official execution. The e-commerce law does not supply notarization, and notarized documents are governed by the Supreme Court's notarial rules. Two e-signatures on an un-notarized deed therefore do not make it a public instrument.

**A is wrong:** this confuses signature with notarization; the Act makes an e-signature equal to a signature, not to a notarial act.

**B is wrong:** even the strongest digital signature proves who signed; it still is not a notarization.

**C is wrong:** the right result for the wrong reason; e-signatures are valid, they simply cannot create a public instrument.

**Watch for:** Verify the current Supreme Court rules on remote and electronic notarization, which may offer a way to notarize electronically.

**Also note:** The Rules on Electronic Evidence treat a document electronically notarized under Supreme Court rules as a public document, and the Supreme Court has since issued rules on electronic notarization (A.M. No. 24-10-14-SC, listed in the 2027 syllabus); this area has changed, so check the current text.

**Basis:** RA 8792, Sec. 7 (proviso); Rules on Electronic Evidence, Rule 5, Sec. 3. Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra2000/ra_8792_2000.html, https://lawphil.net/courts/supreme/am/am_01-7-01_2001.html.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Under the Electronic Commerce Act (RA 8792), a lawyer argues that because the opposing party's evidence is an email, ordinary rules of evidence such as the hearsay rule no longer apply to it. Is the argument sound?

choices.A: Yes; the Act sets aside every rule of evidence for data messages and documents
choices.B: No; the Act changes admissibility rules only on authentication and best evidence
choices.C: Yes; emails are always treated as admissions, so other evidence rules never apply
choices.D: No; emails can never be offered in evidence, so the question does not even arise

questions.explanation:
**B is correct.** The Act deliberately limits its effect on the law of evidence. It changes only the rules on authentication and best evidence, so that electronic records can be proved and treated as originals; it leaves every other statutory rule on admissibility as it was. The purpose is to remove obstacles that arise because a record is electronic, not to create a special zone free of evidence rules. The lawyer's argument would exempt emails from rules the Act never touched, so it fails.

**A is wrong:** the Act's change is narrow, limited to authentication and best evidence; the other rules still apply.

**C is wrong:** nothing in the Act treats every email as an admission; this invents a rule.

**D is wrong:** emails are admissible electronic evidence; the problem is not admissibility in general.

**Watch for:** A question about whether an emailed record is an “original” is testing the best evidence change; one about who wrote it is testing authentication.

**Basis:** RA 8792, Sec. 7; Rules on Electronic Evidence, Rule 1, Sec. 3. Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra2000/ra_8792_2000.html, https://lawphil.net/courts/supreme/am/am_01-7-01_2001.html.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Under the Electronic Commerce Act (RA 8792), an email is admitted in evidence, and the court must now decide how much weight to give it. What does the law tell the court to look at?

choices.A: Whether it was printed on official letterhead before being offered
choices.B: Whether the sender is a corporation or a private individual
choices.C: How reliably it was generated, stored or sent, and how its originator was identified
choices.D: Nothing more, since an admitted electronic record always has full weight

questions.explanation:
**C is correct.** Admission and weight are separate steps: once an electronic record is admitted, the court still decides how much it proves. RA 8792 (Sec. 12) tells the court to look at the reliability of the way the record was generated, stored or communicated, the reliability of the way its originator was identified, and other relevant factors. The Rules on Electronic Evidence (Rule 7, Sec. 1) spell these out further and add the integrity of the system in which the record was kept. These factors target the real risks of electronic records, which can be altered or falsely attributed. So the court looks first at how the email was made and kept and how its sender was identified.

**A is wrong:** letterhead is a paper-world signal; the statute's factors concern how the electronic record was made, kept and attributed.

**B is wrong:** the kind of sender is not a factor; what matters is how reliably the sender was identified.

**D is wrong:** admission does not fix weight; the court must still assess reliability.

**Watch for:** If the email sat in a shared account that anyone could edit, its weight would drop even though it remains admissible.

**Basis:** RA 8792, Sec. 12; Rules on Electronic Evidence, Rule 7, Sec. 1. Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra2000/ra_8792_2000.html, https://lawphil.net/courts/supreme/am/am_01-7-01_2001.html.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Under the Rules on Electronic Evidence and the Electronic Commerce Act (RA 8792), a supplier sues a buyer for breach of a contract made by email and offers printouts of the emails. The buyer objects that the printouts are mere copies and inadmissible. The supplier's IT manager testifies on how the company's email system creates and stores messages. Rule on the objection.

suggestedAnswer.answer: The objection fails. The printouts are treated as originals, and the IT manager's testimony authenticates them.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Under the Rules on Electronic Evidence, a printout or other output that accurately reflects the electronic data is treated as an original (Rule 4, Sec. 1). An electronic document must be authenticated, which can be done through evidence showing its integrity and reliability (Rule 5, Sec. 2). Once it is admitted, the other party may still argue about its weight.
suggestedAnswer.application: First, the printouts reflect the emails stored in the supplier's system, so they are not “mere copies” in the sense of the best evidence rule; they count as originals. Second, the IT manager explains how the system generates and stores emails, which supports their integrity and reliability and so authenticates them. Third, the buyer's remaining remedy is to attack how much the printouts should prove.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion:
The printouts are admissible; the buyer may only contest their weight.

**Common mistake:** applying the paper-based rule that a copy is inadmissible when the original exists, without recognizing that an accurate printout of electronic data is itself an original.

**Watch for:** If the supplier had offered faxed copies instead of printouts of the emails, the answer would change: a fax is treated as a paper copy, not as electronic evidence.

**Basis:** Rules on Electronic Evidence, Rule 4, Sec. 1 and Rule 5, Sec. 2(c). Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/courts/supreme/am/am_01-7-01_2001.html.

keyPoints: An accurate printout of the electronic data counts as an original (REE Rule 4, Sec. 1)
Authentication by proof that the records are intact and reliable (REE Rule 5, Sec. 2(c))
The IT manager's testimony supplies that evidence
The opposing party may contest weight, not admissibility as a copy

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Under the Electronic Commerce Act (RA 8792), Faye, a purchasing officer, approves a purchase order by signing in to her company's procurement portal with her personal account and clicking “Approve.” The supplier later doubts whether this counts as her signature. When does an electronic approval like Faye's equal a handwritten signature?

suggestedAnswer.answer: When it is shown that the approval was made under a set procedure, which the interested parties cannot change, that identifies Faye, is reliable for the purpose, is required before the order can proceed, and lets the supplier check it.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: An electronic signature equals a handwritten one only if it is proved that a prescribed procedure, not alterable by the interested parties, existed under which (Sec. 8): (a) a method identifies the person to be bound and shows her access to the document for giving consent; (b) the method is reliable and appropriate for the purpose, considering all the circumstances and any agreement; (c) signing is necessary for the transaction to go forward; and (d) the other party is authorized and able to verify the signature and decide whether to proceed. All four must be met.
suggestedAnswer.application: First, Faye's personal account identifies her and shows she had access to the order; at the very least, an individual log-in is needed. Second, if the portal is the company's standard, secure procurement system, it is reliable and appropriate for approving orders. Third, the order cannot go through without her approval. Fourth, if the supplier receives the approval and can confirm it came from Faye's account, the verification requirement is met.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion:
If all four requirements are shown, Faye's click is equivalent to her handwritten signature on the purchase order.

**Common mistake:** listing the four requirements without applying each one to the facts, or treating any electronic click as automatically equal to a signature.

**Watch for:** If Faye's team shared one generic account, the identification requirement would fail and the answer would change.

**Basis:** RA 8792, Sec. 8. Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra2000/ra_8792_2000.html.

keyPoints: A prescribed procedure the interested parties cannot alter
(a) Identification and access for consent (at least an individual log-in)
(b) Reliable and appropriate for the purpose
(c) Signing is necessary to proceed
(d) The other party can verify and decide to proceed
All four requirements must be met

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Under the Electronic Commerce Act (RA 8792), a company's signing system identifies the signer, is reliable, and must be used before a deal can proceed, but the other party has no way to verify the signature. Does the signature equal a handwritten one?

choices.A: Yes; meeting most of the requirements is enough for the signature to count
choices.B: Yes; reliability is the only requirement that really matters in the end
choices.C: No; every requirement must be met, including that the other side can verify it
choices.D: No; an electronic signature can never be equal to one written by hand

questions.explanation:
**C is correct.** An electronic signature equals a handwritten signature only when every requirement of Sec. 8 is satisfied: identification, reliability, necessity and verifiability. The requirements work together; each one guards a different risk, and the verification requirement protects the party who relies on the signature. Here three are met, but the other party cannot verify the signature at all. Because one requirement is missing, the signature does not reach equivalence.

**A is wrong:** the requirements are cumulative, not a scorecard; missing any one defeats equivalence.

**B is wrong:** reliability is only one of four; the law separately requires that the other party can verify.

**D is wrong:** the right result for the wrong reason; e-signatures can be equivalent when all requirements are met.

**Watch for:** If the system later gave the other party a way to confirm signatures, the missing requirement would be cured for future transactions.

**Basis:** RA 8792, Sec. 8. Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra2000/ra_8792_2000.html.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Under the Electronic Commerce Act (RA 8792), five employees share one generic account to approve payments in a company system, so any of them can click “Approve.” Which requirement for treating an approval as a person's signature is most clearly in trouble?

choices.A: Identifying which person actually made the approval
choices.B: Showing that the system came from a well-known software company
choices.C: Proving that the payment was large enough to need a signature
choices.D: Showing that each approval was printed and kept in the files

questions.explanation:
**A is correct.** One requirement for an electronic signature to equal a handwritten one is a method that identifies the person to be bound and shows her access to the document for consenting (Sec. 8(a)). At the very least, this calls for an individual log-in, so that each approval can be tied to one person. A shared generic account cannot tell which of five employees clicked. The identification requirement is therefore the one most clearly in trouble.

**B is wrong:** the law is technology-neutral; the vendor's reputation is not a requirement.

**C is wrong:** the size of the payment is not one of the requirements for equivalence.

**D is wrong:** printing is not required; the problem is attribution to a person, not paper records.

**Watch for:** If each employee had a personal account with a password, identification would be satisfied and the analysis would move on to the other requirements.

**Basis:** RA 8792, Sec. 8(a). Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra2000/ra_8792_2000.html.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Under the Electronic Commerce Act (RA 8792), a bank relies on a client's electronic signature to release funds, and the client later denies signing. What does the law presume about the signature?

choices.A: It is presumed forged until the client personally proves that the signature is his
choices.B: It is the client's, made to approve, unless the bank knew of defects or relied unreasonably
choices.C: It is valid in every case, even when the bank already knew it was defective
choices.D: It carries no presumption, so the bank must prove every signature from scratch

questions.explanation:
**B is correct.** The Act (Sec. 9) presumes that an electronic signature belongs to the person it is linked to and that it was affixed to sign or approve the record. The presumption protects people who rely on electronic signatures in good faith, which keeps electronic dealings practical. It does not protect a relying party who knew the signature was defective or whose reliance was unreasonable. So the bank starts with the presumption in its favor, but loses it if it knew of a defect or acted unreasonably.

**A is wrong:** this reverses the presumption; the law presumes the signature is genuine, not forged.

**C is wrong:** the presumption fails when the relying party knew of defects; it is not absolute.

**D is wrong:** the Act does create a presumption in favor of the relying party.

**Watch for:** If the facts showed the bank ignored obvious warning signs, the presumption would fail because its reliance was unreasonable.

**Basis:** RA 8792, Sec. 9. Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra2000/ra_8792_2000.html.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Under the Electronic Commerce Act (RA 8792), Liza pastes a scanned image of her handwritten signature into a PDF contract and emails it. What is the status of that scanned signature?

choices.A: It is automatically equal to her handwritten signature because it is an exact image
choices.B: It is an electronic signature, but whether it equals a handwritten one depends on the process
choices.C: It is not a signature at all and can never have legal effect in any situation
choices.D: It is a digital signature, because a computer was used to scan and paste the image

questions.explanation:
**B is correct.** A scanned image of a signature is a mark in electronic form attached to a document, so it is an electronic signature (Sec. 5(e)). Whether it has the full effect of a handwritten signature depends on the Sec. 8 requirements. A pasted image is usually weak on two of them: it does not reliably show who pasted it, and the other party usually cannot verify it. So it is a signature, but its equivalence is doubtful unless the surrounding process supplies identification and verification.

**A is wrong:** an exact image is easy to copy and paste by anyone, which is why equivalence turns on the process, not the picture.

**C is wrong:** saying it is never recognized is overbroad; it is an electronic signature whose effect depends on Sec. 8.

**D is wrong:** a digital signature uses encryption keys; scanning an image does not make it digital in that sense.

**Watch for:** Verify the current rule: some materials say a scanned signature is simply not recognized, which is broader than the statute supports.

**Basis:** RA 8792, Secs. 5(e) and 8. Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra2000/ra_8792_2000.html.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Under the Electronic Commerce Act (RA 8792), a customer signs up for an online service by clicking “I accept” under its terms. Is the click an electronic signature, and what decides whether it equals a handwritten one?

choices.A: It is not a signature, because the customer did not write or type any name
choices.B: It always equals a handwritten signature, whatever process was used to capture it
choices.C: It is an electronic signature, and its effect depends on the process used to capture it
choices.D: It counts only if the customer later prints the terms and signs them by hand

questions.explanation:
**C is correct.** An electronic signature includes a method or procedure a person adopts with the intention of approving a record. Clicking “I accept” is such a method, so it is a valid electronic signature. Whether it has the full effect of a handwritten signature depends on the process behind the click: whether it identifies the customer, is reliable, is required to proceed, and can be verified (Sec. 8). The answer therefore lies in the process, not in the click itself.

**A is wrong:** an electronic signature need not be a name; a procedure adopted to approve a record can qualify.

**B is wrong:** equivalence is conditional on the Sec. 8 requirements; a weak process may not meet them.

**D is wrong:** requiring a hand-signed printout would defeat the point of recognizing electronic signatures.

**Watch for:** If the click were made from a logged-in account with a confirmation step, the Sec. 8 requirements would be easier to prove.

**Basis:** RA 8792, Secs. 5(e) and 8. Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra2000/ra_8792_2000.html.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Under the Electronic Commerce Act (RA 8792), Paolo electronically signs a one-sided written acknowledgment of a debt, and no other party takes part in the signing. What decides whether his electronic signature can equal a handwritten one?

choices.A: Whether the document is later printed out on paper
choices.B: Whether some other party is able to verify the signature
choices.C: Whether he signed using a government-issued computer
choices.D: Nothing, since one-sided documents always qualify

questions.explanation:
**B is correct.** One of the requirements for an electronic signature to equal a handwritten one is that the other party is authorized and enabled to verify it (Sec. 8(d)). A one-sided document has no built-in counterparty, which makes this requirement the sticking point. It can still be satisfied if some party is able to check the signature. So the deciding question is whether anyone is enabled to verify Paolo's signature.

**A is wrong:** printing does not supply verification and is not a requirement.

**C is wrong:** the device used is irrelevant; the law is technology-neutral.

**D is wrong:** one-sided documents face a real hurdle because the verification requirement still applies.

**Watch for:** If Paolo's creditor received the acknowledgment through a system that let it confirm Paolo's identity, verification would be satisfied.

**Basis:** RA 8792, Sec. 8(d). Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra2000/ra_8792_2000.html.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Under the Electronic Commerce Act (RA 8792), a lending company wants its loan agreements signed online in the way most likely to hold up if a borrower later denies signing. It is choosing among: (1) a typed name below the email message, (2) a signing platform with an audit trail and identity checks, and (3) a digital signature using public-key infrastructure (PKI). Advise the company.

suggestedAnswer.answer: All three are electronic signatures, but a PKI digital signature gives the strongest proof of who signed and that nothing was changed, and a platform with an audit trail is the next best choice.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: An electronic signature equals a handwritten one only if the Sec. 8 requirements (identification, reliability, necessity, verifiability) are proved. A typed name can be an electronic signature (Sec. 5(e)) but does not automatically meet them. Signing platforms help prove the requirements through audit trails and identity checks. A digital signature uses an asymmetric (public-key) system that shows who signed and whether the document was altered afterward; Capalla v. COMELEC recognized such signatures.
suggestedAnswer.application: If a borrower denies signing, the company must prove the Sec. 8 requirements. A typed name gives little evidence of who typed it. A platform's audit trail records identity checks and each signing step, which supports identification and verification. A PKI digital signature goes further by also proving that the agreement was not altered after signing.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion:
The company should use PKI digital signatures where it can, or else a platform with audit trails and identity checks; a typed name alone is the weakest choice.

**Common mistake:** saying that only digital signatures are valid; all three are valid electronic signatures, and the difference lies in how easily the Sec. 8 requirements can be proved.

**Watch for:** If the documents were ones the law requires to be notarized, none of the three would be enough by itself.

**Basis:** RA 8792, Secs. 5(e) and 8; Rules on Electronic Evidence, Rule 2, Sec. 1(a); Capalla v. COMELEC, G.R. No. 201112, June 13, 2012. Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra2000/ra_8792_2000.html, https://lawphil.net/courts/supreme/am/am_01-7-01_2001.html, https://lawphil.net/judjuris/juri2012/jun2012/gr_201112_2012.html.

keyPoints: All three are electronic signatures; equivalence depends on proving the Sec. 8 requirements
A typed name does not automatically meet Sec. 8
Audit trails and identity checks help prove identification and verification
A PKI digital signature proves both identity and integrity (Capalla v. COMELEC)
A clear recommendation ranked by strength of proof

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Under the Electronic Commerce Act (RA 8792), a document is signed with a digital signature. Someone holding the original unsigned document and the signer's public key wants to check it. What can that person find out?

choices.A: The signer's home address and the place where the document was drafted
choices.B: Whether the document was notarized and recorded with a government office
choices.C: The signer's private key itself, so the person can sign documents for the signer
choices.D: Whether the signer's private key was used, and whether the document was later altered

questions.explanation:
**D is correct.** As explained in Capalla v. COMELEC, a digital signature is an electronic signature created by transforming a document with an asymmetric (public-key) system. The signer uses a private key; others use the matching public key to check the result. Someone with the original document and the public key can therefore tell whether the transformation was made with the signer's private key and whether the document was changed after it was signed. That is why digital signatures prove both identity and integrity.

**A is wrong:** a digital signature proves the key used and the document's integrity, not personal details like an address.

**B is wrong:** notarization and registration are separate formalities that a digital signature does not show.

**C is wrong:** the private key is never revealed by the public key; that secrecy is the whole basis of the system.

**Watch for:** If the document had been changed after signing, the check would show the mismatch, which is why digital signatures are strong evidence of integrity.

**Basis:** Capalla v. COMELEC, G.R. No. 201112, June 13, 2012. Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/judjuris/juri2012/jun2012/gr_201112_2012.html.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Under the Electronic Commerce Act (RA 8792), election returns are signed electronically when the board chairperson uses a device holding a digital certificate and the board members enter PINs issued by the election body, before the returns are transmitted. A losing candidate claims the returns were never validly signed. Following Capalla v. COMELEC, how should this be resolved?

choices.A: The returns were validly signed, because the certificate-and-PIN procedure meets the law
choices.B: The returns are void, because election returns must always be signed by hand
choices.C: The returns are valid only if each member also signs a printed copy of them
choices.D: The returns are void, because a PIN cannot serve as a signature under any law

questions.explanation:
**A is correct.** An electronic signature may take the form of a distinctive mark or sound in electronic form, or of a method or procedure a person adopts with the intention of approving or authenticating a record. In Capalla v. COMELEC, the Court held that the digital certificates in the devices, the PINs, and the procedure used to turn each election return into a digitally signed document before transmission complied with the law. The candidate's claim assumes a signature must be a handwritten mark. Under the Court's reasoning, the procedure itself is the signature, so the returns were validly signed.

**B is wrong:** this ignores that a method or procedure adopted to authenticate a record can be an electronic signature.

**C is wrong:** the Court found the electronic procedure sufficient on its own; no printed copy was required.

**D is wrong:** a PIN used as part of an authentication procedure can form part of an electronic signature.

**Watch for:** If the board had skipped the PIN step, the procedure would be incomplete and the claim would deserve a closer look.

**Basis:** Capalla v. COMELEC, G.R. No. 201112, June 13, 2012. Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/judjuris/juri2012/jun2012/gr_201112_2012.html.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Under the Electronic Commerce Act (RA 8792), Dina orders a phone on a shopping app by tapping the purchase button and paying online. The seller later refuses to deliver, claiming there is no contract because nobody signed anything. Is the seller right?

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. A contract made through electronic means is not invalid simply because it is electronic or unsigned, as long as its essential elements are present.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Under RA 8792 (Sec. 16(1)), unless the parties agree otherwise, every element of a contract, offer and acceptance included, may be shown through electronic records, and being electronic is never by itself a reason to treat a contract as invalid. A consensual contract such as a sale does not need a signature unless the law requires a particular form. The essential elements of a contract must still be present.
suggestedAnswer.application: The seller's app offered the phone at a price, and Dina's tap on the purchase button and her payment expressed her acceptance. Consent, a definite object and a price are all present. Nothing in the law requires a signature for this sale, and the electronic form of the exchange is not a ground to deny it effect.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion:
A valid contract of sale was formed; the seller must deliver the phone.

**Common mistake:** stopping at “electronic contracts are valid” without checking that the essential elements of the contract are actually present.

**Watch for:** If the app had only displayed the phone with “price on request,” there would be no definite offer to accept, and the analysis would change.

**Basis:** RA 8792, Sec. 16(1); Civil Code, Arts. 1318 and 1356. Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra2000/ra_8792_2000.html, https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra1949/ra_386_1949.html.

keyPoints: Sec. 16(1): contract elements may be expressed and proved electronically
No contract is denied validity just because it is electronic
A consensual contract needs no signature unless the law requires a form
The essential elements must still be present, and are present here

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Under the Electronic Commerce Act (RA 8792) and the Civil Code, a seller emails an offer to sell a machine on Monday; the buyer emails an unqualified acceptance on Tuesday, which the seller reads that afternoon; on Wednesday the seller emails that it is withdrawing. When was the contract perfected?

choices.A: On Monday, as soon as the seller sent its offer to the buyer by email
choices.B: On Wednesday, because the seller could still withdraw until it confirmed
choices.C: On Tuesday, once the acceptance created consent on the machine and its price
choices.D: Never, because email contracts need a signed paper copy to be perfected

questions.explanation:
**C is correct.** RA 8792 lets offer and acceptance be made through emails (Sec. 16(1)), but it does not change when a contract is perfected; that is still governed by the Civil Code. A consensual contract is perfected by the meeting of the minds on its object and cause (Arts. 1305, 1315, 1319). The buyer's unqualified acceptance, read by the seller on Tuesday, completed that meeting of minds. A withdrawal on Wednesday comes after perfection and cannot undo the contract.

**A is wrong:** an offer alone is not a contract; perfection needs an acceptance.

**B is wrong:** after an unqualified acceptance, no further confirmation is needed; the withdrawal is too late.

**D is wrong:** email contracts are perfected like any consensual contract; no paper copy is required.

**Watch for:** If the buyer's Tuesday reply had changed the price, it would be a counter-offer, not an acceptance, and the seller's Wednesday withdrawal could prevent any contract.

**Basis:** RA 8792, Sec. 16(1); Civil Code, Arts. 1305, 1315 and 1319. Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra2000/ra_8792_2000.html, https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra1949/ra_386_1949.html.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Under the Electronic Commerce Act (RA 8792), two businesses agree by email on a service contract, and neither signs anything, not even electronically. No law requires a special form for this kind of contract. Is it valid?

choices.A: Yes; a consensual contract needs no signature when no special form is required
choices.B: No; every contract must be signed by both parties before it can take effect
choices.C: No; email contracts take effect only once notarized under the Act
choices.D: Yes; the e-commerce law treats every email contract as already notarized

questions.explanation:
**A is correct.** A consensual contract is perfected by consent and is valid without a signature, unless a law requires a particular form for it. RA 8792 recognizes contracts formed through data messages (Sec. 16(1)), so the email exchange can show the parties' consent. Here no special form is required. The contract is therefore valid even though no one signed it.

**B is wrong:** signatures are needed only where the law requires a particular form; consensual contracts do not.

**C is wrong:** the e-commerce law does not require or supply notarization for ordinary contracts.

**D is wrong:** the right result for the wrong reason; the Act never turns an email into a notarized document.

**Watch for:** If the law required this contract to be in a public instrument, the email exchange would not be enough for that form.

**Basis:** RA 8792, Sec. 16(1); Civil Code, Art. 1356. Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra2000/ra_8792_2000.html, https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra1949/ra_386_1949.html.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Under the Electronic Commerce Act (RA 8792), two companies' framework agreement says any future order binds them only if signed on paper. One company later accepts an order only by email. Is the order binding?

choices.A: Yes, because the law forbids parties from refusing to contract electronically
choices.B: Yes, because an email acceptance always overrides any earlier agreement on form
choices.C: No, because electronic acceptances are never valid between private companies
choices.D: Not under their agreement, since parties may agree to exclude electronic means

questions.explanation:
**D is correct.** The rule that offers and acceptances may be made electronically (Sec. 16(1)) applies “unless otherwise agreed.” The law makes electronic contracting available, but it respects the parties' freedom to choose another method for their own dealings. These companies agreed that orders bind only when signed on paper. An email acceptance does not meet the method they chose, so under their own agreement the order is not binding.

**A is wrong:** the law permits electronic contracting; it does not force it on parties who agreed otherwise.

**B is wrong:** the statutory default yields to the parties' agreement, not the other way around.

**C is wrong:** the right result for the wrong reason; electronic acceptances are generally valid, but not here because of the agreement.

**Watch for:** If the framework agreement were silent on form, the email acceptance would be effective.

**Basis:** RA 8792, Secs. 16(1) and 38. Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra2000/ra_8792_2000.html.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Under the Electronic Commerce Act (RA 8792), a buyer chats a seller, “Nice bag, I might get it next month,” and the seller replies, “Sure, just tell me.” The seller later claims a sale was made through the chat. Is there an electronic contract?

choices.A: No; being electronic does not remove the need for a real offer and acceptance
choices.B: Yes; any chat exchange about a product creates a binding electronic sale
choices.C: Yes; the seller's reply is an acceptance, so the sale was perfected at once
choices.D: No; a sale can never be made through a chat app, only through a website

questions.explanation:
**A is correct.** RA 8792 lets contracts be formed and proved electronically, but it does not create contracts where the essential elements are missing. A sale still needs consent, shown by a definite offer and an unqualified acceptance, on a definite object and price. “I might get it next month” is an expression of interest, and the seller's reply only invites a later order. With no real offer and acceptance, no contract was formed, whatever the medium.

**B is wrong:** the medium does not supply consent; the messages must still amount to offer and acceptance.

**C is wrong:** there was no definite offer to accept; the buyer only expressed possible future interest.

**D is wrong:** the law is technology-neutral; a sale can be made through chat if the elements are present.

**Watch for:** If the buyer had written “I'll take it for ₱3,000” and the seller replied “Deal,” a sale would be perfected through the chat.

**Basis:** RA 8792, Sec. 16(1); Civil Code, Arts. 1318–1319. Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra2000/ra_8792_2000.html, https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra1949/ra_386_1949.html.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Under the Electronic Commerce Act (RA 8792), once a cash withdrawal through an inter-bank ATM network is consummated, what one bank owes the other because of it is absolute and cannot be put through ____ of credits.
questions.fullText: Under the Electronic Commerce Act (RA 8792), once a cash withdrawal through an inter-bank ATM network is consummated, what one bank owes the other because of it is absolute and cannot be put through preference of credits.
questions.explanation:
**Answer:** preference.

**Why:** Transactions through bank networks are consummated when cash is actually dispensed, or when one account is debited and another credited (Sec. 16(2)). The Act then makes the resulting obligation between the banks absolute and exempts it from preference of credits, the process of ranking creditors' claims. This keeps the network reliable: a bank that paid out cash for another bank's depositor can count on being reimbursed in full. The term that completes the phrase is therefore “preference.”

**Not to be confused with:** “concurrence.” Concurrence and preference of credits are usually discussed together, but the Act specifically shields these obligations from the preference process, so “preference” is the only term that fits.

**Watch for:** If the question asked when the transaction is consummated rather than how the obligation is treated, the answer would be the moment cash is dispensed or the accounts are debited and credited.

**Basis:** RA 8792, Sec. 16(2); Civil Code, Book IV, Title XIX (concurrence and preference of credits). Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra2000/ra_8792_2000.html, https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra1949/ra_386_1949.html.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Under the Electronic Commerce Act (RA 8792), a depositor withdraws cash from another bank's ATM through a shared network. At what point is the transaction considered done?

choices.A: When cash is actually dispensed, or one account is debited and another credited
choices.B: When the depositor enters the correct PIN and selects the amount
choices.C: When the bank lists the withdrawal on the monthly account statement
choices.D: When the depositor signs a printed receipt and returns a copy to the bank

questions.explanation:
**A is correct.** For transactions made through networks linking banks, the Act fixes the moment of consummation (Sec. 16(2)): the actual dispensing of cash, or the debit of one account with the corresponding credit to another. A clear rule matters because several institutions are involved and each needs to know when its obligation became final. In a cash withdrawal, the deciding moment is when the machine releases the cash. Once that happens, the transaction is consummated.

**B is wrong:** entering a PIN only starts the transaction; consummation comes with dispensing or debit and credit.

**C is wrong:** the statement only reports a transaction that was already consummated earlier.

**D is wrong:** ATM transactions involve no signed receipt; the Act ties consummation to the movement of money.

**Watch for:** If the machine failed to release the cash and no account was debited, the transaction would not be consummated.

**Basis:** RA 8792, Sec. 16(2). Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra2000/ra_8792_2000.html.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Under the Electronic Commerce Act (RA 8792), two companies are setting up an electronic ordering system between them. Who decides what type and level of security (passwords, encryption, consent prompts) their transactions will use?

choices.A: The DTI, which sets one required security standard for everyone
choices.B: The courts, which must approve the method before any transaction
choices.C: No one, since every deal must use a public-key digital signature
choices.D: The two companies themselves, choosing whatever suits their needs

questions.explanation:
**D is correct.** The Act leaves it to the parties to decide how much security their electronic dealings need and which technical methods to use (Sec. 24). This fits the law's technology-neutral approach: different transactions carry different risks, so the law does not impose one method on everyone. The companies may agree, for example, on consent prompts or on limiting what information is collected. The choice is theirs to make.

**A is wrong:** the Act does not impose a single government standard; it leaves the choice to the parties.

**B is wrong:** there is no requirement of prior court approval for security methods.

**C is wrong:** a digital signature is one strong option, not a requirement for every transaction.

**Watch for:** If a dispute later arises, the chosen method still matters, because it affects whether signatures and records can be shown to be reliable.

**Also note:** The freedom is not unlimited: it is subject to applicable laws and to rules and guidelines the DTI issues with other agencies.

**Basis:** RA 8792, Sec. 24. Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra2000/ra_8792_2000.html.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Under the Electronic Commerce Act (RA 8792), a shipper and a carrier handle a shipment entirely electronically: the carrier confirms loading by email, and the shipper later transfers its right to claim the goods through the carrier's online system. The consignee refuses to deal with the electronic records, insisting that these steps must be done on paper. Is the consignee right?

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. The Act lets actions connected with a contract of carriage of goods be done through data messages or electronic documents, even where a law requires writing or paper.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: RA 8792 applies to actions connected with a contract of carriage of goods, such as confirming that goods have been loaded, claiming delivery, and transferring rights in the goods (Sec. 25). Where the law requires such an action to be done in writing or with a paper document, using data messages or electronic documents satisfies the requirement (Sec. 26(1)). Where a right must pass to one person only, the electronic method must make the data message unique (Sec. 26(3)).
suggestedAnswer.application: Confirming loading and transferring the right to claim the goods are both actions listed in Sec. 25. Even if a law required them to be in writing or on paper, Sec. 26(1) treats the electronic records as satisfying that requirement. Because the right to claim the goods must belong to one person, the carrier's system must make the transfer unique, so that the right cannot be duplicated.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion:
The consignee's objection fails, provided the system keeps the transferred right unique.

**Common mistake:** assuming that documents of title must always be on paper, without applying Secs. 25–26.

**Watch for:** If the parties had switched back to paper documents midway, Sec. 26(5) would require the electronic records to be terminated and the paper to state that termination.

**Basis:** RA 8792, Secs. 25–26. Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra2000/ra_8792_2000.html.

keyPoints: Sec. 25: the Act covers actions connected with carriage of goods (loading, delivery claims, transfer of rights)
Sec. 26(1): writing or paper requirements are met by data messages or electronic documents
Sec. 26(3): a right that must pass to one person requires a unique data message
Application to each step in the facts

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Under the Electronic Commerce Act (RA 8792), where only one person may hold the right to claim shipped goods, the electronic method used for the transport document must make the data message ____.
questions.fullText: Under the Electronic Commerce Act (RA 8792), where only one person may hold the right to claim shipped goods, the electronic method used for the transport document must make the data message unique.
questions.explanation:
**Answer:** unique.

**Why:** Some rights in the carriage of goods, such as the right to demand delivery, can belong to only one person at a time. On paper, that is guaranteed by there being a single original document. Electronic records can be copied endlessly, so the Act requires the electronic method to make the data message unique, ensuring that only one person can exercise the right. “Unique” is therefore the required quality.

**Not to be confused with:** “authentic.” Authenticity shows a message is genuine and from the stated sender, but a genuine message can still be copied; uniqueness is what prevents two people from holding the same right.

**Basis:** RA 8792, Sec. 26(3). Checked against the official text: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra2000/ra_8792_2000.html.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
